Laboratory-reared Golden topminnow, Fundulus chrysotus, were monitored to document early growth trajectories under stable thermal conditions. At 91 days post-hatching, individuals attained a total length of 3.75 cm , a value derived from standard length measurements and indicative of relatively rapid juvenile development. The wet weight of newly emerged yolk-sac larvae, based on the reported egg diameter of 2.6 mm in the related species Fundulus parvipinnis, was estimated at 0.0092 grams [Wwb = 0.0092 grams]. This modest initial mass reflects the small, energy-dense yolk reserves typical of cyprinodontiform embryos, which sustain the larva through the endotrophic phase until the onset of exogenous feeding at the time of mouth openingnan. The period between eclosion and first prey capture is brief, a critical window during which the mouth opens and the digestive tract becomes functional.

Evaluations of reproductive capacity in F. chrysotus were conducted at a water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], conditions that match the species' typical spring breeding temperatures in the southeastern United States. Under this thermal regime, mature females produce 245 eggs per year [Ri = 245 eggs per year] across multiple spawning events, each clutch containing approximately 15 to 20 demersal, adhesive eggs. This annual output aligns with values documented for the congener Fundulus catenatus, suggesting a conserved life-history strategy within the genus. Spawning is asynchronous and occurs over an extended breeding season lasting several months, with individual females releasing multiple small clutches of eggs that become attached to submerged vegetation; the estimated frequency is roughly 10 to 15 clutches per year [F_R_i = roughly 10 to 15 clutches per year]. The eggs are transparent and undergo rapid cleavage-stage development.

Longevity records for Fundulus chrysotus maintained at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] indicate that individuals can survive for 730 days [am = 730 days] under controlled conditions, a lifespan that likely overestimates survival in the wild due to the absence of predation and environmental stressors. Nonetheless, this maximum recorded longevity provides a useful benchmark for demographic modeling and population projection. The time elapsed since birth at puberty for F. chrysotus raised at the same temperature (20 °C [T = 20 °C]) is 305 days since birth [tp = 305 days since birth], a duration that corresponds to the onset of vitellogenesis and the first appearance of mature gametes in the gonads. This pubertal timeline, occurring roughly ten months after hatching, underscores a relatively fast maturation schedule compared to larger-bodied fundulids, which may require multiple years to reach reproductive competence.

As the fish continue to grow beyond the pubertal stage, their body size gradually approaches an asymptotic maximum. The ultimate total length attained by mature individuals is 8.88 cm [Li = 8.88 cm], a value consistent with the species' position as a medium-sized member of the topminnow guild. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight of an adult F. chrysotus is approximately 12.9 grams [Wwi = approximately 12.9 grams], a mass that reflects the allometric scaling relationship between length and weight derived from the observed length-weight power function. This asymptotic body mass is achieved only after the allocation of resources shifts from somatic growth toward gamete production, resulting in a plateau in the growth curve that is typical of determinate-growing fish species. Field-collected specimens approaching this upper size limit are rarely encountered, suggesting that only a small fraction of the cohort survives to reach full adult dimensions.

Comparisons between the early growth data and the mature size estimates reveal a striking developmental plasticity in F. chrysotus. The initial mass of 0.0092 grams [Wwb = 0.0092 grams] represents less than 0.1% of the ultimate adult mass of 12.9 grams [Wwi = 12.9 grams], highlighting the extreme ontogenetic growth trajectory that spans more than three orders of magnitude. This dramatic biomass increase is supported by a high annual egg production of 245 eggs per year [Ri = 245 eggs per year] at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], which compensates for the substantial juvenile mortality typical of small-bodied freshwater fishes. The entire life cycle, from hatching through senescence at 730 days [am = 730 days], is thus completed within a relatively compressed temporal window for a fish of this size, reflecting a strategy that prioritizes early maturation and high fecundity over extended somatic growth at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C].
